content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided recommendations for the use of linezolid in tuberculosis (TB) treatment regimens. Evidence supporting these recommendations focused on regimens that included bedaquiline, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, clofazimine, and linezolid. Secondary analyses of longer regimens containing both bedaquiline and linezolid demonstrated favorable outcomes. The inclusion of linezolid was intended to strengthen the regimen, particularly to protect bedaquiline, while awaiting drug susceptibility testing results for resistance to fluoroquinolones and other drugs. However, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) advised against including linezolid in shorter, all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimens until further evidence becomes available. Countries are encouraged to explore modified regimens containing both bedaquiline and linezolid under operational research conditions. Routine drug susceptibility testing (DST) is critical for patient selection and monitoring the development of drug resistance. Although no major safety risks were identified in the data reviewed, active TB drug safety monitoring and management systems must be in place to detect, manage, and report adverse events and drug toxicities promptly. The GDG identified several research priorities to address gaps in evidence for managing multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). These include studies comparing shorter, all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline and linezolid with other companion drugs, as well as studies focusing on specific subgroups such as pregnant or lactating women. Randomized controlled trials and operational research are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of these regimens and to better understand mechanisms of resistance to bedaquiline. Efforts should also focus on standardizing data collection to contribute to global recommendations. The Nix-TB study, conducted in South Africa, evaluated a 6–9 month regimen (BPaL) consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid for patients with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or treatment-intolerant or non-responsive MDR-TB. The study demonstrated high treatment success rates but also highlighted significant adverse events, particularly related to linezolid. Peripheral neuropathy was reported in 69% of patients, and anemia in 37%. Linezolid-related toxicities were dose-dependent, with higher toxicity rates observed at higher daily doses. Close monitoring of hemoglobin levels and peripheral neuropathy is recommended, as these conditions are often reversible with dose adjustments or discontinuation. The GDG acknowledged the high success rates of the BPaL regimen but noted the uncertainty of evidence due to the high rate of adverse events. Only 18% of patients completed the full 1200 mg/day dose of linezolid. The panel emphasized the need for further research to optimize dosing and reduce toxicity. Concerns about potential male infertility associated with linezolid, observed in animal studies, were also raised, though human data are not yet available. Overall, while shorter regimens like BPaL show promise in improving treatment outcomes for drug-resistant TB, challenges remain in balancing efficacy with the management of adverse effects.
